title: Yahweh Led Me All the Way — an Oath, a Well, a Leading
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Today we come to the longest chapter in Genesis — sixty-seven verses of it. And all that length, from the first verse to the last, is spent on one single errand: an old servant with no name sets out from home to find a wife for his master's son.
Why would the author spend so much space on it? Because this chapter is answering a question that every one of us has asked at some point.
How do you know God is leading you? Some people say you wait for a feeling of peace. Some say you wait for a confirmation. And some simply say: I can't tell, so I may as well decide for myself.

And the sentence at the centre of this chapter is one the servant himself says: "As for me, Yahweh has led me on the way." The Hebrew word order is stronger still: I was on the way — and Yahweh led me.

Let me put the answer up front. God's leading is given to people who are moving; it is not given to people who sit still and wait for it to arrive. And a real confirmation has never been a lucky coincidence. It is character, seen in a person.
1. An Old Man Putting His Affairs in Order
Verse 1: "Abraham was old, and well advanced in age. Yahweh had blessed Abraham in all things."
Brothers and sisters, "in all things" — בַּכֹּל (*bakol*) — is the closing summary of that promise back in 12:2, "I will bless you." A whole lifetime, and it came true.

And what is it that weighs most on an old man who has been blessed all his life? Verse 2: "Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had, 'Please put your hand under my thigh.'"

That posture for taking an oath occurs only twice in the whole book: here, and in 47:29, where Jacob makes Joseph swear. Both times it is about the same enormous matter — the offspring, and the promise.

And what is the oath he wants sworn? Verses 3 and 4: "…you shall not take a wife for my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I live. But you shall go to my country, and to my relatives, and take a wife for my son Isaac."

Brothers and sisters, notice "my country … my relatives" — אַרְצִי … מוֹלַדְתִּי — these are precisely the two words God used in 12:1 when he told him to leave. The place he is sending his servant back to is the very place he himself was called out of.

Why? Not because of bloodline. Rebekah is just as much a foreigner as anyone else; she simply is not a Canaanite. The dividing line is which God is worshipped — the worship of the Canaanite gods involved temple prostitution and the sacrifice of children, and the book of Judges shows with perfect clarity what happens once the two are mixed. And later on Rahab is a Canaanite and Ruth is a Moabite, and both of them are written into the genealogy of the Lord Jesus.
And verse 8 contains a remarkably mature sentence: "If the woman isn't willing to follow you, then you shall be clear from this oath to me."

Brothers and sisters, he is confident, and he does not force it. He believes God will bring it about, and at the same time he leaves the other person's freedom intact. That sentence is worth copying out by everyone who prays for a child, for a fellow worker, or for a marriage of their own.
Abraham makes his servant swear, "You shall not take a wife for my son of the daughters of the Canaanites." Isn't that simply exclusion?

It depends on the reason. What he says next is, "But you shall go to my country, and to my relatives, and take a wife for my son Isaac" — and the decisive thing there is not bloodline, it is the environment of faith. Canaanite religion included temple prostitution and the offering of children in sacrifice; that is the kind of thing that pulls a whole household away. And the principle the rest of Scripture works with is the same one: 2 Corinthians 6 says, "Don't be unequally yoked with unbelievers" — a line drawn around faith, not around ethnicity. So the right application today is this: when you choose whom to marry, look at faith and at values, not at nationality, skin colour or family standing. To use this passage to prop up the exclusion of a people group is a complete misuse of it.
What if a Christian is already married to someone who does not believe — how should this chapter be read then?

Very carefully, and never as a verdict. 1 Corinthians 7 could hardly be plainer: "if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she is content to live with him, let him not leave her … For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband." That is to say, for someone already inside a marriage the teaching of Scripture is: stay, and love well. 1 Peter 3 goes further, and says an unbelieving husband may "be won by the behavior of their wives without a word." So the people this chapter addresses are the ones who have not yet decided; those who are already inside should be hearing those other passages. Pastorally we must be especially watchful here — do not let this lesson become a thorn in somebody else's household.
2. A Light from the Original: Led While on the Way
From verse 10 on, the servant sets out with ten camels and arrives at the city of Nahor, at evening, "the time that women go out to draw water."
Verse 12, and he prays: "Yahweh, the God of my master Abraham, please give me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham."

Verse 14, and he asks for a sign: "Let it happen, that the young lady to whom I will say, 'Please let down your pitcher, that I may drink,' then she says, 'Drink, and I will also give your camels a drink,' — let her be the one you have appointed for your servant Isaac."
Brothers and sisters, this sign deserves a careful look, because it is very often learned wrongly.

What he asks for is not a random coincidence — not "if that young woman is wearing blue", and not "if it rains tomorrow, then it is God's will." What he designs is an action that will bring a person's character into the open.

Do the arithmetic. Ten camels, at the end of a long trek; a single camel can drink a hundred litres of water. And the pitcher has to be let down into the well and hauled up again, trip after trip after trip. If a young woman actually says, "I will also give your camels a drink," what she is committing herself to is an hour or two of drawing water — for an old man she has never met in her life.
So that is not the drawing of lots. That is a test of character.
And verse 15 says, "Before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah came out … with her pitcher on her shoulder."
The prayer was not yet finished, and the answer was already on its way.
And then comes verse 27, the sentence at the centre of the whole chapter: "As for me, Yahweh has led me on the way to the house of my master's relatives."
The Hebrew word order runs like this: I was on the way, and Yahweh led me.
Brothers and sisters, take hold of that order. He did not see the whole route first and then set out. He set out first, and then he was led while he was on the way.

And notice what this entire chapter is missing. No vision. No dream. Not one word spoken by God. In verse 7 he does mention that God "will send his angel before you" — and that angel never once walks onto the stage, from beginning to end.

So how does the leading in this chapter actually happen? He prays. He travels. He watches. He opens his mouth and asks. He negotiates. He gives thanks. The leading of God is hidden inside those very ordinary movements.
The old servant prays beside the well and asks for a sign. Was that a right way to pray?

This passage often gets misused as a template for "asking God for a confirmation", so we need to see the difference clearly. The sign he asks for is not random: he asks for a piece of behaviour that will reveal character — a young woman who not only gives him a drink but goes on, of her own accord, to draw water for ten camels. Watering ten camels until they are full means hauling up dozens of bucketfuls; that is not a coincidence, it is evidence of diligence and of mercy. So what he is really asking for is, "Let me see who this person is." And that is intensely practical for us: rather than praying for a signal to drop out of the sky, pray that God would let you see a person's character clearly. Notice too that he prays and moves at the same time — the text says that before he had finished speaking, Rebekah came out.
"Yahweh has led me on the way" — is leading something you know before you walk, or only something you know after you have walked?

That sentence in verse 27 is the key: "As for me, Yahweh has led me on the way." In the original it runs, I was on the way, and Yahweh led me. He says it afterwards, looking back down the road he has already travelled. And that is an enormous release for us: most people assume they must see the whole road before they dare move, and yet the pattern Scripture gives is this one — led while on the way. So the practical thing to do is to take the step you are already sure of; the leading very often shows up only at the next junction. This is not, of course, a licence to be reckless. He set out with a clear commission, with clear principles, and with clear prayer.
3. A Man Who Never Mentions His Own Name
Brothers and sisters, now I want to point out the thing in this chapter that is most easily read straight past.
The most important human figure in the whole chapter — and Scripture never once writes down his name.

He is called "Abraham's servant", and "the man", and "his servant, the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had." Some have guessed that he is the Eliezer mentioned in 15:2, but in this chapter the text deliberately declines to say.

And what is even more worth noticing is the way he talks. Verse 34: "I am Abraham's servant." Verse 35: "Yahweh has blessed my master greatly." And then for a dozen verses and more he retells his master's words sentence by sentence — how blessed his master's son is, and how God led him on the road.
In that whole speech he says "my master" more than ten times, and he mentions himself only in the words "I am the servant."

Brothers and sisters, this is one of the clearest samples of selflessness anywhere in Scripture. It is not that he has no ability — he brings the entire errand off. It is not that he carries no weight — the whole estate is in his hands. He simply steps back, so that what people see is his master.
And in John 16:13–14 the Lord Jesus describes the Holy Spirit like this: "he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak … He will glorify me."

And there is one more detail, in verse 33: "Food was set before him to eat, but he said, 'I will not eat until I have told my message.'" He will not so much as eat first. The errand comes ahead of his own need.
The chapter keeps withholding the servant's name. Is that deliberate?

His name never appears in the whole chapter; he is only ever "the servant" and "the man" — the text plainly has no intention of making him the leading figure. And he does exactly the same thing himself. He comes into somebody's house, food is set in front of him, and he says, "I will not eat until I have told my message." And when he does tell it, he begins with "I am Abraham's servant", and everything he says from there on is about his master and about God. It is an exquisite pattern of service: make yourself small in the telling, and make the one who sent you large. For anyone who serves today the reminder is very direct — it is no bad thing for a congregation to remember your name, but if you stand in the middle of the picture the whole time, the one who sent you is blocked from view.
Verse 50, and Laban and Bethuel say, "The thing proceeds from Yahweh. We can't speak to you bad or good." Verse 51: "Behold, Rebekah is before you. Take her, and go."
And then in verse 55 the family says, "Let the young lady stay with us a few days, at least ten" — which is the most natural human feeling in the world.
And then verses 57 and 58: "We will call the young lady, and ask her … They called Rebekah, and said to her, 'Will you go with this man?' She said, 'I will go.'"
Brothers and sisters, sixty-seven verses long, and all the negotiating, the praying, the retelling and the bargaining is done by men. And the shortest speech in the chapter is hers — three words.
In Hebrew it is a single word: אֵלֵךְ (*elech*).

And weigh those three words for a moment. She is to leave her country, her relatives and her father's house, to travel off with an old servant she met that same day, to marry a man she has never laid eyes on — and never to come back.
That is the same thing God said to Abram in 12:1. And what the text writes over Abram is, "So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him"; what it records of her is, "She said, 'I will go.'"

Brothers and sisters, in every generation somebody has to be willing to say those words. The line of the promise carries on not because the previous generation was magnificent, but because in the next generation somebody was willing to get up and go.
And the chapter closes at verse 67: "Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah's tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife. He loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death."

Notice the order there: she became his wife, and he loved her. The covenant first, and the feeling afterwards. That is the exact reverse of the order our own age works with — we take the feeling first and discuss the commitment later. And here Scripture holds out another possibility: love can also begin as a decision, and then grow into an affection.
Rebekah says "I will go" — how could she possibly decide that fast?

Verse 58: "They called Rebekah, and said to her, 'Will you go with this man?' She said, 'I will go.'" In the original that is a single word, אֵלֵךְ. And that one word stands on the same line as Genesis 12, where God tells Abram to leave his country, his relatives and his father's house, and the text then says, "So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him" — she too is someone who leaves home for a place she has never seen. So with that one word the text sets her among the ranks of faith. As for how quickly it happened, we need neither defend her nor dress it up; the text records only what she said. What is there to learn is the sheer decisiveness of it: once she knew, she went.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is to preach "asking for a sign" as a transferable method for seeking guidance. This servant travelled first, prayed first and watched first — and what he asked for was a test of character, not a random coincidence. Preach it as a method and the congregation will start treating God as a box of lots: "if it rains tomorrow, that is God's will." New Testament believers have the Holy Spirit living within them and the whole of Scripture in their hands; making lot-drawing the normal way to seek guidance very easily turns into a way of shifting responsibility off oneself.

The second is to preach this chapter straight off as a guide to choosing a spouse. It does have to do with marriage, but the main line running through it is God's leading and the continuation of the line of promise. Shrink it into a technique for finding a partner and the single brothers and sisters will walk out more anxious than they came in — as though God had already appointed one particular person and they had simply failed to find them.

The third is to preach "do not take a Canaanite wife" as a distinction of race. What Abraham cared about was the direction of a household's faith, not its bloodline. 2 Corinthians 6:14 says, "Don't be unequally yoked with unbelievers" — that is a boundary drawn around faith, not a boundary drawn around a people. Preach it wrongly and you will raise up a faith with a sense of superiority baked into it.

The fourth is to skip over the fact that the servant has no name. The most important human figure in the chapter, and Scripture never once writes his name down — that is deliberate. Skip it, and you have left out one of the clearest samples of selflessness in the Bible.

The fifth is to preach "the thing proceeds from Yahweh" as though whatever goes smoothly must be God's will. When Laban said that sentence, there was a gold ring in front of him, and bracelets, and costly gifts — and the chapters that follow tell us plainly enough what kind of man Laban turned out to be. A smooth road does not necessarily mean God's will, and a hard road does not necessarily mean God is barring the way. The standard for discerning is whether the thing itself squares with Scripture, and whether it grows the likeness of Christ in a person.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: Chinese parents are often deeply involved in a child's marriage, sometimes to the point of naming the person. Does this chapter support parents deciding? Brothers and sisters, there are three things to see clearly here. First, Abraham did take the initiative and make the arrangement — that was the norm of his age. But notice where he draws his line: in verse 8 he says, "If the woman isn't willing to follow you, then you shall be clear from this oath to me." He holds a view, and he does not compel. Second, the text goes out of its way to record verses 57 and 58: the family calls the young woman in, they ask her what she wants, and she answers for herself. In an age when marriages were settled by the head of the house, the author has deliberately left the speaking to her. Third, what Abraham cared about was not family standing, not property, not education, but the direction of faith. So the lesson this chapter sets for Chinese parents is not "you may not have an opinion." It is this: put your standard on faith and on character, and leave the deciding to your child.

The second question: I am praying about something — how do I tell whether it is God's leading or my own idea? Brothers and sisters, this chapter hands us four very practical checks. First, have I set out? God leads people who are moving. If you do nothing at all and simply wait for a voice, in all likelihood no voice will come. Second, am I asking for a coincidence, or for character? The sign the servant designed was an action that would show what was in a person's heart. If you are praying "if such and such happens, then that is what God means", ask yourself first: what would that thing actually reveal? Third, where will this take me? The servant walked the whole way to the house of his master's relatives — the direction matched what his master had told him. God's leading will never carry you to a place that contradicts Scripture. Fourth, is anyone else looking at this with me? The servant went in and retold the whole affair to both households. 1 Corinthians 14:29 says, "let the others discern." A "leading" that you dare not set in front of your spiritual companion usually needs to wait a little longer.
Where is the line between praying for a child's marriage and deciding it for them?

Look at the three things this chapter actually does. First, the father settles a principle — the environment of faith — and not a person; he never names which young woman it has to be. Second, the servant, once he is there on the ground, does not decide for anyone either; he asks God to make it plain, and even at the end he still has to ask Rebekah herself, "Will you go with this man?" Third, the family too is asked what it thinks. So the whole affair has a principle in it, a seeking in it, and the consent of the person concerned. The line today can follow those same three layers: state the principle clearly — and state it early, and state it often; let the child meet and decide on the person themselves; and then honour what they want. The most powerful influence a parent has is not naming the partner. It is living out a home the child would want to reproduce.
7. Living 321 Out — Step Back, So That People See the Lord
Brothers and sisters, let us join this lesson back onto the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — the old servant never mentions his own name; he speaks only his master's words, and the only son he praises is his master's. And the Lord Jesus says of the Holy Spirit that "he will not speak from himself … He will glorify me." Brothers and sisters, my role model is this: the one who serves steps back, so that people see the Lord. And that is very concrete — when you share something, what the people listening remember afterwards, is it your story, or is it that Lord?

The Bible is my standard — the most interesting thing about this chapter is that the standard does not rest on a voice out of heaven; it rests on words the master had already spoken. From beginning to end the servant is simply carrying out those two sentences in verses 3 and 4. That is exactly what a standard is for: on the days when there is no miracle, you still have in your hand a word that has already been said.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — look again at verse 27: I was on the way, and Yahweh led me. Guidance mostly happens out on the road, not in a meeting room. If you know for certain which direction you should be going, then go; a great many things only come clear once you are standing beside that well.

Let Jesus be King — verse 8: "If the woman isn't willing to follow you, then you shall be clear from this oath to me." Brothers and sisters, that is a remarkably mature sentence: he is certain of God's heart, and he does not manipulate the outcome. To let Jesus be King is to do my own part to the full, and then to leave another person's free will with God. When you pray for your child, for your spouse, for a fellow worker, this is the sentence to learn.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — verse 52: "When Abraham's servant heard their words, he bowed himself down to the earth to Yahweh." The errand has succeeded, and the first thing he does is put his face on the ground. And back in verse 26, at the moment the answer came beside the well, he had already "bowed his head, and worshiped Yahweh." That man worshipped twice on that journey, and said his own name zero times.

Establish God's system — when Rebekah says "I will go", she is facing the same direction as God's call to Abram in chapter 12. Brothers and sisters, in every generation somebody has to be willing to say those words. To establish God's system is to hand this line on — and the way you hand it on is not by deciding for the next generation, but by living out the kind of life that makes them willing to say, "I will go."

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We put a great deal of weight on selflessness, and this chapter gives us both an excellent sample of it and a necessary clarification: the servant's selflessness is not an absence of conviction, or of ability, or of judgement. He designed the test. He negotiated. He insisted on finishing his message before he would eat. He refused to be held back for ten days. The man was extremely capable; he simply would not put the credit on himself. So selflessness is not the same thing as incompetence, and it is not the same thing as having no opinion. A person who shelters under the word selflessness and will not carry responsibility for anything is not being selfless. That is avoidance.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same Well
Brothers and sisters, one prayer beside one well — and falling into four different kinds of heart, it teaches four completely different things.

The proud heart learns a method: "So that is how you ask for a sign." This heart reads the chapter as a piece of technique. Brothers and sisters, notice that the real leading figure in this chapter is a man who does not even have a name. If what you most want to learn when you close the chapter is how to ask, rather than how to step back, you have probably taken the wrong thing out of it.

The fearful heart learns anxiety: "How do I know I asked for the right thing?" This heart will seek confirmation about a decision until it no longer dares to move at all. To that heart I want to say: look at the order in verse 27 — he was led while he was on the way. You do not have to be certain of the whole route; you only have to move on the one point you already know. And notice this as well: before he ever asked for that sign, he had already travelled several hundred kilometres.

The ashamed heart learns to think little of itself: "Someone like me — God would probably never lead me that way." Brothers and sisters, look carefully at whom God used in this chapter. He did not appear to Abraham. He did not speak to Isaac. The one he led was an old servant with no name. The most delicate leading in the chapter, God gave to the person of lowest standing in it.

The wounded heart learns suspicion: "Rebekah was asked what she wanted exactly once — did she really have a choice?" That is an honest question, and I want to point out two things. First, the text deliberately records that one question, and it leaves the words "I will go" to her — in that age, writing it that way was taking a position. Second, this chapter never pretends the road was an easy one. She left everything, went to a place she had never seen, and married a man she had never seen. Her "I will go" cost her exactly what Abraham's "so he went" cost him. God sees what that costs.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, set out. Find one thing where you already know the direction and have been waiting for "a clearer confirmation", and this week take the first step in it. God's leading is given to people who are moving.

Second, change the shape of what you ask for. If you are seeking confirmation about a decision this week, do not ask, "Which one is more to my advantage?" Ask instead, "Which one would bring character into the open?" That is how the servant designed his sign.

Third, practise stepping back. This week, tell someone about something God has done, and deliberately leave out how much it cost you. See how hard that is — because that is what the servant does for a whole chapter.

Fourth, pray for one person, and at the same time leave that person's freedom with God. Pray once in the pattern of verse 8: "Lord, I ask you to bring it about; and if he will not, I will not force it."

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences: the longest chapter in the Bible is about an old servant with no name who goes out to find a wife for his master's son; there is no vision in the whole chapter and God never speaks, the man simply prays, travels and watches, and at the end he says, "I was on the way, and Yahweh led me"; and the shortest sentence in the chapter belongs to the young woman — "I will go."
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that leading is given to those who are moving; I will move on the one point I already know.
I declare that the confirmation I ask for is not coincidence but character.
I declare that I will do my own part to the full and not manipulate the outcome; another person's freedom I leave with God.
I declare that I will step back, so that what people see is my Lord and not me.
I am to "take a step first" this week — but what if I take the wrong one?

Start by separating two kinds of step. The first kind is the big irreversible one — getting married, resigning, signing a contract, moving house. Those need to be slow: seek God over them, talk them through with people who have experience, leave yourself time. The second kind is the small reversible one — going to see somebody, asking a question, signing up for a course, beginning a settled time of prayer. Those you can simply go and take; if one of them turns out wrong, the loss is limited. Most people's paralysis comes from hesitating over a small step as though it were a big one. This week, take only a step of the second kind. And remember that sentence: he was led while he was on the way. He did not wait until he had it all worked out at home.

Brothers and sisters, if only two sentences from this lesson may remain, I want to keep the one spoken by the man who talks the longest in this chapter, and the three short words spoken by the one who talks the least.
The old servant said, "As for me, Yahweh has led me on the way."
One of them was led while he was on the way; the other stood at the junction and said, I will go.

Brothers and sisters, put those two sentences together and you have everything this chapter has to teach us: God's leading falls on the people who are willing to set out, and God's plan is carried on in the hands of the people who are willing to get up and go.

And there is one more thing I want you to see. Verse 63 says, "Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the evening." And it was while he was meditating that he lifted up his eyes and saw the camels coming.
He had no idea that this would be the day his life turned a corner. He simply did what he always did, and went out at evening to be quiet.
And while he was meditating, God brought the answer right up in front of him.

Brothers and sisters, this is the tenderest detail in the chapter: on one side a man running a thousand miles, on the other a man meditating in a field — and God joined the two lines together in one and the same evening.

The focus is not on whether I asked for the right sign, not on whether I can see the whole route, and not on whether my name is left behind when my life is over. The focus is on Jesus — he is the Lord who sends, who leads, and who brings it about himself. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to set out on the one point we already know, and, when evening comes, to go outside and be quiet a while. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ "Yahweh has led me on the way" — is leading something you know before you walk, or only after you have walked? How does that change the way you wait?
2. ★★ The sign the servant asked for was a piece of behaviour that revealed character, not a random signal. What is the difference between those two?
3. ★ The whole chapter withholds the servant's name. What kind of service does that way of writing let you see?
4. ★★ The father sets the principle, the servant asks God to make it plain, and the person concerned says "I will go" for herself. How do those three layers apply in a family today?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I can arrange this better than God can), fearful (one wrong step and it is all over), ashamed (I made the wrong choice back then), wounded (my own marriage was decided for me by somebody else). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read this aloud: "As for me, Yahweh has led me on the way." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there something in your hands right now that you have been waiting to "see the whole of" before you dare move? Is that thing reversible, or irreversible?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The reason I most often use to put off a step I ought to take is …"
9. ★★ This week, which "small reversible step" are you going to take? Say the time, the place and the person.

Leader's reminder: be especially careful when the talk turns to marriage and to choosing a partner. There may be brothers and sisters in the group who are single, who are divorced, or who live with an unbelieving spouse. Do not let the discussion turn into people appraising one another, and do not let this lesson be read as a verdict on anyone.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, which principle is it that you need to state earlier and state more clearly to your children or to the younger ones?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your ministry, what is there that you ought to be letting the person concerned decide for themselves?
